P1.claim: N on EXACT >= N off EXACT + 15 pp

P5.claim: median DIST N on < N off

n1.how: I read each hex value in my head. I estimated the red, green and blue levels, the hue, how light it was and how saturated. Then I matched that to common English colour words, adding a modifier for lightness or brightness.

n2.how: I read each hex triplet, judged the relative red, green and blue amounts to place the hue, then judged lightness and saturation. I picked familiar English colour words, with modifiers to tell apart the many close greens.

n3.how: I estimated hue, lightness and saturation from each hex's red, green and blue bytes in my head. Then I matched them to common English colour words and picked different names for the similar greens.

n4.how: I read each hex value in my head, judged its hue, lightness and saturation, and gave it a common English colour name. Several of these values match names I remember from the xkcd colour survey (apricot, apple green, light peach, indigo blue), so I used those names where they fit.

n5.how: I read each hex value's red, green and blue parts by eye. I judged hue from which channels were strongest, lightness from the overall size of the values, and saturation from how far apart the channels were. Then I picked a familiar plain-English colour word for each.

n6.how: I read each hex value as red, green and blue amounts and pictured the colour. Where a code matched a crowd-sourced colour name I already knew, like apricot, apple green or indigo blue, I used that name. For the others I described the hue, how light it is and how strong it is.

s1.how: I looked once at the card image and named each chip by eye. I picked a common English colour name for its hue, then added a word for lightness or saturation (dark, light, bright, muted) where that helped tell similar chips apart.
s1.tools: Read (the file-reading tool), used once to view card.png. No other tools, programs, files or searches.

s2.how: I viewed the card once and named each chip by eye. I picked a common English colour word for the hue, then added a lightness or saturation word (light, dark, bright, dusty) where it helped tell similar chips apart, especially the many greens.
s2.tools: Read (the file-reading tool), used once to view card.png. Nothing else.

s3.how: I looked at the card image once and named each chip by eye, choosing common English colour words for its hue, lightness and saturation. Where chips looked alike, such as the several greens, I set them apart with modifiers like bright, dark or yellowish.
s3.tools: Read (file-reading tool, used once to view card.png)

s4.how: I opened the card image once and looked at each chip. I named each colour by eye, using common colour words for its hue, lightness and saturation. I added modifiers like "dark" or "pale" so that similar chips get different names.
s4.tools: Read (file-reading tool), used once to view card.png

s5.how: I viewed the card image once and named each chip from how it looked, using common English colour words for its hue, lightness and saturation. I adjusted names so the many greens could be told apart (grass, kelly, forest, emerald, olive, leaf, apple, lime, neon).
s5.tools: Read (file-reading tool, used once on card.png)

s6.how: I opened the card image once and looked at each numbered chip, judging hue, lightness and saturation by eye, then picked the common English colour name that best fit. Where neighbouring greens looked alike, I separated them by brightness and by how yellow or blue they leaned.
